Florence, March. Pietro's school is taking part in the "Guides for a day" project at the Uffizi. Pietro and Davide have chosen Filippo Lippi's Madonna and Child with two angels, the painting Bellini's grandfather took Bellini to see as a child. They rehearse with Bellini, in the gallery.
So: this is Filippo Lippi's Madonna. It's very beautiful.
"Very beautiful" says nothing. Whoever is listening must be able to see it with their eyes closed. Let's start with the composition: what's in the foreground?
In the foreground, on the right, there are two angels lifting the Child. On the left, in profile, the Madonna with her hands joined.
And in the background, behind a window, there's a landscape: rocks, a river, a distant city.
Good. And the light? Where does it come from?
From the left. It makes the Madonna's veil stand out, which is almost transparent.
And the angel at the bottom? Is he looking at the Child?
No! He turns his gaze towards us. And he's smiling. One would say he's about to laugh.
It's as if he wanted to step out of the painting to play with whoever is looking.
There. First describe, then interpret. "It seems", "one would say", "it's as if": they're honest words. They say it's your impression, not a truth.
Professor, when your grandfather brought you here, what did he say to you?
Just two words. "Look. And don't touch anything." It took me sixty years to understand that the second part was the less important.
Stress on "RO": ci-ce-RO-ne. Both "c"s soft, as in "cheer".

The project was called "Guides for a day" and the Uffizi Gallery organised it every spring with the city's secondary schools. For a whole Saturday, the pupils became guides in the museum: each chose a work, studied it for two months, and on the appointed day explained it to visitors, who stopped to listen if they wished. Pietro's class had been given the early Renaissance corridor. His classmates chose Botticelli, Paolo Uccello, Piero della Francesca. Pietro and Davide, who despite attending different schools had asked to work as a pair, chose a smaller painting, hanging in a corner of the Filippo Lippi room: a Madonna and Child with two angels, painted around 1465, which Florentines affectionately call "the Lippina". None of the teachers understood why they had chosen that one. Pietro didn't explain. It was the painting in front of which, sixty years earlier, Ernesto Bellini had led his five-year-old grandson by the hand.

Bellini told Pietro about it one winter evening, at the trattoria, when he heard about the project. He was five, he said, and it was 1969. His grandfather, who had spent the years after the flood washing mud off hundreds of paintings, took him to the Uffizi one Tuesday morning, when the museum was almost empty. They crossed room after room without stopping, his grandfather with his hat in his hand and him struggling to keep up. Then his grandfather stopped in front of that small painting, knelt down to his height and said just two words: "Look. And don't touch anything." They stayed there for half an hour, in silence. "He didn't explain anything to me," said Bellini. "He didn't tell me who the painter was, or when he painted it, or what it meant. He let me look. It was the most important lesson of my life. And for sixty years I believed it was a lesson about not touching."

For two months, Pietro and Davide studied the Lippina as they had never studied anything. Pietro read everything he could find: the life of Filippo Lippi, a Carmelite friar who fell in love with a nun, Lucrezia Buti, and married her, scandalising Florence; the theories according to which the Madonna in the painting has Lucrezia's face and the Child that of their son, Filippino, who also became a painter. Davide, on the other hand, copied it. He went to the Uffizi every Saturday morning, with a special permit obtained thanks to Chiara, sat on a folding stool in front of the painting and drew for three hours. In two months he made eleven copies: in pencil, in charcoal, in watercolour, in tempera. Each copy was more precise than the one before. "Copying is the slowest way of looking," he said. "And so the best."

It was during the ninth copy that Davide noticed something he hadn't read in any book. In the right eye of the angel at the bottom, the one who smiles, there was a tiny white dot, a reflection of light the size of a pinhead. He drew it, then looked more closely with the magnifying glass Karl had lent him, and realised the reflection wasn't a dot: it was shaped like a small rectangle, with a cross in the middle. It was the window. The same window as in the background, the one opening onto the landscape, reflected in the angel's eye. Davide ran to Chiara with the drawing. Chiara looked, then phoned a colleague at the Uffizi, who confirmed it: it was a detail known to specialists, but almost no visitor saw it. "Lippi put the window in the angel's eye," Davide told Pietro that evening, his eyes shining. "It means the angel is looking out. Towards us. The painter did it on purpose."

The first version of Pietro's explanation was full of information and almost empty of painting. It talked about Lippi, Lucrezia, the Medici, dates, attributions, studies. When he read it to Bellini, in the gallery, on a Tuesday morning like the one in 1969, the old restorer listened to the end with his eyes closed. Then he opened them and asked: "And the painting, where is it?" Pietro didn't understand. "You spoke for ten minutes," said Bellini, "and with my eyes closed I saw nothing. I don't know where the Madonna is, what colour her cloak is, where the angel is looking. Whoever listens to you must be able to see the painting even if they have their back to it. First describe. Then tell the story. Stories are only useful after someone has looked." Pietro went home, threw away the first version and started again from scratch.

The second version began like this: "In the centre of the painting, on the left, we see the Madonna in profile, seated on a carved wooden chair, with her hands joined in prayer. She wears a blue dress and a very light veil, almost transparent, adorned with pearls, which covers her gathered blonde hair. In the foreground, on the right, two child angels lift the Baby Jesus towards her, and he stretches his arms out to his mother. The angel at the bottom, his wings barely visible, looks neither at the Madonna nor at the Child: he turns his gaze towards us, and smiles. In the background, behind the Madonna, a window opens onto a landscape: rocks, a flowing river, a distant city in the mist. The light comes from the left and makes the Madonna's veil and face stand out, so that they seem almost to shine." Bellini listened to it with his eyes closed. When Pietro had finished, he smiled. "Now I can see it," he said.

Davide, meanwhile, was preparing a surprise he hadn't revealed to anyone, not even Pietro. He had read somewhere that some museums had raised reproductions of famous paintings, for blind visitors, and had asked Chiara whether the Uffizi had one of the Lippina. They didn't. So he decided to make one himself. He took his best copy, the pencil one, transferred it onto thick card and went over every line with a thin strip of PVA glue, which as it dried became a ridge you could feel with your fingers. Then he glued on pieces of different fabric for the various parts: velvet for the Madonna's dress, gauze for the veil, very fine sandpaper for the rocks of the landscape. It took him three weeks. When he showed it to Chiara, she touched it with her eyes closed, for a long time. Then she said only: "Bring it. You'll need it on Saturday."

The Saturday of the guides came at the end of March, on a sunny day that made Florence look freshly painted. Pietro and Davide arrived at the Uffizi at eight, an hour before opening, with badges round their necks saying "Guide" and a folder full of notes that neither of them would consult. They took up position in front of the Lippina, one on the right and one on the left, like two sentries. At a quarter past nine the first visitor arrived: a German gentleman with a guidebook in his hand, who looked at them suspiciously. Pietro began explaining in English, his hands trembling. The gentleman listened for one minute, then two, then five, and in the end closed his guidebook. When Pietro had finished, the gentleman looked at the painting for a while longer, then said in hesitant Italian: "I have seen this painting three times in my life. Today is the first time I see the angel who smiles."

Around ten, among the visitors, Pietro recognised a familiar face, half hidden behind a column and an open guidebook: it was Professor Ruggeri, who had come from Rome without telling anyone. He listened to Pietro's explanation from beginning to end, at the back of the group, pretending to be an ordinary tourist. When Pietro finished and asked, as he always did, whether anyone had questions, Ruggeri raised his hand. "Just one," he said. "Why does the angel look at us and not at the Child?" Pietro recognised him, blushed, and then answered calmly: "I don't know for certain. But Davide discovered that the window is reflected in his eye. One would say the painter wanted the angel to look out of the painting. It's as if he were inviting us in." Ruggeri nodded, closed his guidebook and left without saying anything more. Later Pietro found a note slipped into his folder: "Cautious answer. Interesting hypothesis. Pass. R."

During the morning dozens of people came. A Japanese honeymoon couple, who photographed Pietro instead of the painting. A schoolteacher from Prato with twenty eight-year-olds, who sat on the floor and asked questions about everything: why the angels were children, why the Madonna wasn't looking at her son, why the Child was so chubby. Davide answered the question about the chubby Child by saying that in the fifteenth century a chubby child was a healthy child, and that thin children frightened mothers. The children laughed. An American lady asked whether the painting was for sale. A Fine Arts student asked Davide if she could see his copies, and spent twenty minutes leafing through them. Around midday, Pietro noticed something strange: the more he explained the painting, the more he saw it. Every time he described it to someone, he discovered a new detail. A flower on the window sill. A pearl on the veil. A reflection in the angel's eye.

The most important visitor of the day arrived at three in the afternoon. He was an elderly gentleman, tall and thin, in a grey coat, with a white cane and a guide dog, a honey-coloured labrador who sat down neatly at his feet. He was accompanied by a younger woman, his daughter. The gentleman stopped in front of the Lippina, or rather in front of the spot where his daughter told him the Lippina was, and asked in a calm voice: "I've been told there's a boy here who explains it well. I haven't been able to see for twenty years. But I saw this painting when I was young, many times. I used to teach it to my students. I was an art history teacher at a secondary school. Could you describe it to me? I'd like to see whether I still remember it." Pietro felt his throat go dry. He turned to Davide. Davide, without a word, opened his folder and took out the card with the raised drawing.

The gentleman's name was Alberto. Pietro described the painting to him slowly, with the words of the second version, but more slowly, pausing after every sentence, as Bellini had taught him. While Pietro spoke, Davide guided Signor Alberto's fingers over the card: here the Madonna, in profile; here the joined hands; here the veil, made of gauze, which felt very light; here the angels, here the Child with his arms outstretched; here the window, and behind it the sandpaper rocks. Signor Alberto touched in silence, his head slightly tilted, as if listening to music. When his fingers reached the angel at the bottom, Pietro said: "This angel isn't looking at the Child. He's looking at us. And smiling. One would say he's about to laugh. It's as if he wanted to step out of the painting to play with whoever is looking at him." Signor Alberto's fingers stopped on the angel's face, and stayed there.

"Yes," said Signor Alberto after a long silence. "I remember. That angel. I used to call him 'the cheeky angel', with my students. I used to say he was the only angel in Italian painting who wanted to play a prank." He smiled, and for a moment his face resembled the angel's. "For twenty years I've tried to remember his face and couldn't any more. Today I've seen it again." His daughter had tears in her eyes. The guide dog, which until then had stayed motionless, got up and rested its muzzle on Davide's knee. Signor Alberto asked Pietro his name, and what he wanted to be when he grew up. Pietro said he didn't know yet. "It doesn't matter," said Signor Alberto. "Whatever you do, keep describing things like this. There's always someone who can't see them. And it isn't always because they're blind."

Before leaving, Signor Alberto touched the card once more, from beginning to end, as you reread a letter. Then he asked Davide whether he could keep it. Davide hesitated for a second: it was three weeks' work. Then he gave it to him, wrapped in paper. Signor Alberto took it with both hands, as you take something fragile. Two weeks later, a letter arrived at the Uffizi addressed to the management, signed by Alberto Ricci, retired teacher. It told the story and asked the museum to consider creating raised reproductions for blind visitors, "like the one a fifteen-year-old boy made with glue and fabric". The management replied that the project would be launched the following year. And it asked Davide, through his school, whether he would like to take part as a consultant.

When Davide told his mother, Rita sat down on the sofa and was silent for a minute. Then she asked him what "consultant" meant. Davide explained that they would call him in to give advice on how to make paintings touchable, for people who can't see. Rita looked at him for a long time, that son who four years earlier had drawn on the courtyard walls and whom she saw only in the mornings, coming back from her night shift. "I spend my nights at the hospital," she said quietly, "holding the hands of people who are afraid of the dark. And now you do the same thing, but with paintings." Davide had never thought of it that way. That evening, in his sketchbook, he drew two hands: a nurse's, with a wedding ring, and a child's, holding a pencil. The hands barely touched, above a small smiling angel.

In the afternoon, while Pietro and Davide were still in front of the Lippina, the whole family arrived. Matei and Giulia with Viola, who was almost six and had never been to the Uffizi. Graziella, who hadn't set foot in the Uffizi since 1975, "when I went with Aldo the day before the wedding". Chiara and Karl. And last of all Bellini, with his stick, walking slowly and stopping in every room. Before reaching the Lippina, Giulia took Viola into the Botticelli room, in front of the Primavera. Viola stood open-mouthed in front of that garden full of figures, flowers and orange trees. "Which one is me?" she asked, because she knew her name came from there. Matei knelt beside her and pointed to the figure dressed in flowers, on the right, scattering roses on the meadow. "That's Flora," he said. "But look at her feet. Do you see those little purple flowers on the meadow? They're violets. We named you after them."

Viola looked at the violets for a long time, then asked Pietro, who had joined them, to explain the painting to her the way he explained it to visitors. Pietro tried. But the Primavera wasn't his painting, and after three sentences he got muddled between the Graces, Mercury and Zephyr. Viola interrupted him. "I'll do it," she said. And she began describing it her own way, with the serious air of a guide: "In the foreground there are lots of flowers. In the centre there's a lady who looks sad. Above her there's a child with arrows who's about to do something naughty. On the right there's a blue man who looks like a ghost and wants to catch a girl. The girl is scared and flowers come out of her mouth." She stopped. "And in the background there are oranges. It's as if it were summer, but it's called spring." A group of tourists who had stopped to listen applauded. Viola took a bow.

Then they all reached the Lippina. It was almost closing time, and the room was quiet. Graziella sat down on the velvet bench in front of the painting, because her feet hurt, and looked at it in silence. After a while she said something nobody expected: "Aldo brought me here. In front of this one. The day before the wedding." Everyone turned round. "He told me that Madonna had the face of a nun who had married a painter, and that all Florence had made a scandal of it, but that he found her the most beautiful Madonna in the world because she was a real woman, not a saint." She stopped, looked at the transparent veil. "I told him I had no time for Madonnas, that I had a trattoria to run. He laughed. He said: 'Look at her anyway. Just one minute.' I looked at her for a minute. I had forgotten. Until now."

Pietro felt something tighten in his chest. His grandfather Aldo and Ernesto Bellini in front of the same painting, a few years apart, with the same word: look. He turned to Bellini, who had come up to the painting leaning on his stick. "Professor," he said, "would you like me to explain it to you?" Bellini looked at him in surprise. Then he nodded and closed his eyes. And Pietro, in front of the whole family, explained the Lippina for the last time that day. He told them about the composition, the light, the colours, the veil, Signor Alberto's cheeky angel. Then he told the story of Lippi and Lucrezia, of Ernesto and the five-year-old boy, of Aldo and Graziella the day before the wedding. When he finished, Bellini opened his eyes. They were moist. "It's the first time in sixty years anyone has explained it to me," he said. "My grandfather never explained it to me. He was right: at five you just have to look. But at sixty-five, every now and then, it's nice to listen too."

Then Bellini did something Pietro never forgot. He turned to Viola, who had sat down on the floor in front of the painting, cross-legged, exactly as Bellini must have sat in 1969. With difficulty, leaning on his stick and on Matei's shoulder, he knelt beside her, to get down to her height. Viola looked at him, curious. Bellini pointed at the painting and said a single word: "Look." Then he fell silent. Viola waited. "And then?" she asked. Bellini smiled. "And then nothing," he said. "My grandfather also said 'don't touch anything'. But I've understood it isn't needed. Whoever looks carefully has no need to touch." Viola looked. She looked for a whole minute, in silence, which for a girl of almost six was an eternity. Then she pointed at the angel at the bottom. "He's looking at me," she said. "I know," replied Bellini. "He looks at everyone who looks at him."

While Matei helped him up, Bellini took Pietro by the arm and drew him a little aside, by the window of the room. He spoke in a low voice, so the others wouldn't hear. "Do you know why my grandfather took me to this painting in particular?" he asked. Pietro shook his head. "He told me many years later, shortly before he died. In November 1966 this painting was in a storeroom on the ground floor. It was one of the first to be saved from the water, and he was among those who carried it up the stairs, by hand, in the dark. Three years later he wanted his grandson to see it dry, clean, in its place. It was his way of telling me that things can be saved." He stopped, looked at Viola sitting on the floor. "One day it will be your turn," he said. "You'll bring someone here. A boy, a girl. Don't explain anything, the first time. Just tell them: look." Pietro promised. He wrote it that very evening, in the black notebook, under the date.

The attendant announced closing time. They all left together, slowly, through the long corridor with the statues, to the terrace from which you could see Palazzo Vecchio lit by the setting sun. Davide walked ahead with Karl, telling him about Signor Alberto. Chiara and Giulia talked about the tactile reproductions project. Matei carried Viola on his shoulders. Graziella walked arm in arm with Bellini, slowly, both with sticks, hers the one Guido had given her for her birthday. Pietro stayed a little behind. He stopped at the last window of the corridor, from which you could see the Arno, the Ponte Vecchio and, on the other side, the roofs of the Oltrarno. He looked for via Maggio, the trattoria, the workshop. He couldn't find them, they were hidden among the roofs. But he knew they were there. And for the first time he thought that his city, too, was a painting, with a foreground, a background and a light coming from the left.

That evening, at the trattoria, Graziella served everyone ribollita and then sat down, a rare thing, at the big table with them. On Doina's embroidered tablecloth, Davide laid the eleventh copy of the Lippina, the watercolour one, the best, and gave it to Graziella. "For the shelf," he said. "Next to Aldo." Graziella looked at it for a long time. Then she stood up, went into the kitchen and pinned it above the shelf, next to the photographs of Aldo and Viorica, Pietro's crooked cup, the plaque, the page with the review, the sarmale recipe. "By now," she said, coming back to the table, "there's more history in that kitchen than at the Uffizi." Bellini laughed. "And more people looking at it," he said. "Which, for a painting, is the most important thing." Viola, who had fallen asleep on the bench with her head on Giulia's lap, smiled in her sleep, like the cheeky angel.

Before going to sleep, Pietro opened the black notebook at the first page, the one Bellini had written in 1987 and which contained a single sentence of grandfather Ernesto's: "Look carefully." He had never really noticed it. He reread it. Then he leafed through the notebook from the beginning, page after page: the dome, the diaries, the Bridge of Lies, the child's fingerprint, the Madonna with two faces, the Master's hand, the red bicycle, the sarmale. All the pages said the same thing, in different ways. At the end he wrote the date, and below it a description. Not of a painting. Of the day. "In the foreground: a blind gentleman touching an angel's face and remembering it. In the centre: a little girl sitting on the floor looking for a whole minute. In the background: an old man kneeling, a grandmother remembering, a boy describing. The light comes from the left. It's as if the whole painting said a single word." He wrote it at the bottom, in capitals: "LOOK."
